## Which way do Cook pines lean?

![From Johns *et al.* (2017): "Typical cultivated stand of *Araucaria columnaris* at the University of California, Irvine campus"](../img/johns-etal-2017-fig1.jpeg){width=40%}


Consider small random sample ($n = 5$)

> -0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20

```{r}

df <- data.frame(y = c(-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20))

ybar <- mean(df$y)
s <- sd(df$y)
s2 <- var(df$y)

```



## The sampling distribution of the difference between sample and population mean

We want to know the sampling distribution for the difference between sample mean $\overline{Y}$ and the population mean $\mu$

$Z$-standardization gives us a standard normal sampling distribution (mean = 0, sd = 1):

$$Z = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\sigma_{\overline{Y}}}$$

BUT, we don't know the population standard error of the mean $\sigma_{\overline{Y}}$, we have to estimate from the sample $\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$.



## Student's $t$ distribution {.t}

The $t$ distribution accounts for the fact that we have to estimate both $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from the sample

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}}$$

$t$ is like $Z$ except there is uncertainty about the sample standard error



## Student's $t$ distribution

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="75%"}


df1 <- crossing(x = seq(-4, 4, 0.01), nesting(
  Distribution = c("t", "Z"), 
  df = c(4, Inf))) %>%
  mutate(y = dt(x, df))

ggplot(df1, aes(x, y, color = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 2) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c(parse(text = c("italic(t)[4]")), parse(text = c("Z")))) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)~or~italic(Z))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18)
  )

```


## \alert{One-sample $t$-test}

> The \alert{one-sample $t$-test} compares the mean of a random sample for a normal population with the population mean proposed in a null hypothesis

## Null hypothesis testing

1. State null and alternative hypotheses
2. Calculate test statistic
2. Identify null distribution 
3. Calculate $P$-value
4. Decide:

    - Reject null
    - Fail to reject null


## 1. Null and alternative hypotheses

$H_0$: The true (population) mean equals $\mu_0$

$H_A$: The true (population) mean does not equal $\mu_0$

Often, $\mu_0 = 0$, like in our example:

$H_0$: The mean axial lean is 0 ($\mu = 0$)

But $\mu_0$ could be something else depending on what you're testing

## 2. The $t$ test statistic

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu_0}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}}$$



## Which way do Cook pines lean?

> `-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20`

| $\overline{Y}$     | $s$             | $s^2$            |
|:------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------:|
| `r round(ybar, 3)` | `r round(s, 3)` | `r round(s2, 3)` |



$$\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{`r round(s, 3)`}{\sqrt{5}} = `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`$$

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu_0}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}} = \frac{`r round(ybar, 3)` - 0}{`r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`} = `r round(ybar/ (s/sqrt(5)), 3)`$$



## 3. The $t$ distribution is the sampling distribution for $t$

Remember: the $t$-distribution comes from the standard normal, but with added uncertainty about the standard deviation.

We *estimate* the standard deviation, and account for its uncertainty, with a \alert{$\chi^2$ distribution}. 

Thus our $t$-distribution has degrees of freedom: $df = n - 1$

For our study, $5 - 1 = 4$ degrees of freedom

## 3. The $t$ distribution is the sampling distribution for $t$

The $t_4$ distribution looks like this:

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

test_stat <- ybar / (s / sqrt(5))

df <- tibble(t = seq(-4, 4, 0.01), y = dt(t, 4))

alpha <- 0.05
critical_value <- qt(
  p = alpha / 2,
  df = 4, # n = 5, df = n - 1
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = test_stat, size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```



## 4. $P$-values

\alert{One-sample $t$-test} is usually two-sided because we would be equally surprised by a positive or negative difference from $\mu_0$

The $t$ distribution is symmetrical around 0, so we can find the area under of the curve greater/less than and our test statistic and use that same value, times -1, on the other side

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t > test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t < -test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(test_stat, -test_stat), color = "grey", size = 2) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```

## 4. $P$-values

For a two-tailed test (most common)

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}

P_value <- 2 * pt(
  q = 1.592,
  df = 4,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

P_value
```

## 4. $P$-values: Even easier with the function `t.test`

```{r echo = TRUE}
y <- c(-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20)
t.test(y)
```

## 5. Decide

Since $P = `r round(P_value, 3)`$ is greater than $\alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

We don't have enough evidence to conclude that Cook pines lean towards the equator from this sample

## Confidence intervals for the mean

Check it out, given to us by `t.test`:

```{r}
t.test(y)
```

## 95% confidence intervals for the mean

Recall definition of confidence intervals: 95% of the time, 95% confidence intervals will include the true population mean

## 95% confidence intervals for the mean

$$-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} < \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}} < t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}}$$

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="75%"}

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t < critical_value, t > -critical_value), fill = "tomato") +

  geom_vline(xintercept = c(critical_value, -critical_value), color = "grey") +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  geom_label(
    data = tibble(t = c(-critical_value, critical_value), y = rep(0.3, 2),
                  label = c("-italic(t)[list(0.05(2),4)]", "italic(t)[list(0.05(2),4)]")),
    mapping = aes(label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 10
  ) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )


```




## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}

$$\overline{Y}-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}< \mu < \overline{Y}+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$$

For $n = 5$, we have 4 degrees of freedom, so we calculate $t_{0.05(2),4}$

```{r echo = TRUE}
critical_value <- qt(0.025, 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
critical_value
```



 
## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}


$$\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`$$
$$t_{0.05(2),4} = `r round(critical_value, 3)`$$


Lower 95\% CI: $`r round(ybar, 3)` - `r round(critical_value, 3)` \times `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)` = `r round(ybar - critical_value * s/sqrt(5), 3)`$

Upper 95\% CI: $`r round(ybar, 3)` + `r round(critical_value, 3)` \times `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)` = `r round(ybar + critical_value * s/sqrt(5), 3)`$
  


## Great! What if I want to compare **two** variables?

## Great! What if I want to compare **two** variables?

Two-sample t-test to the rescue

## There are two ways to compare two means

* \alert{Paired $t$-test} provides a control for extraneous
variation and therefore have more power and precision.

* \alert{Two-sample $t$-tests} are often easier because you do not have to resample the same unit as in a paired comparison.

> In the *paired* design, both treatments are applied to every sampled unit. In the *two-sample* design, each treatment group is composed of an independent, random sample of units

## \alert{Paired $t$-test}

We used a \alert{paired $t$-test} to compare stomatal traits on the upper and lower surface of the same leaves. The sampled units are the species, the treatments are the leaf surface

Because each member of a pair shares much in common, researchers can ignore extra variation (e.g. difference in stomatal traits among species) and just focus on effect of treatment

Examples of paired comparisons:

* Before and after treatment
* Clones one with a treatment and one without

## \alert{Paired $t$-test}

> Paired measurements are converted to a single measurement by taking the difference between them

In other words, a \alert{paired $t$-test} is a one-sample $t$-test

* The null hypothesis of difference in means is denoted $\mu_{d0}$
* Degrees of freedom is number of pairs $- 1$

## Assumptions of \alert{Paired $t$-test}

* Pairs are randomly sampled from a population
* The differences are normally distributed

Does NOT assume that individual values are normally distributed


## Confidence intervals for the difference in means

Identical to confidence intervals for mean of a single sample

We just replace $\overline{Y}$ with $\overline{d}$, $\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$ with $\text{SE}_{\overline{d}}$, and $\mu$ with $\mu_d$

## 95% confidence intervals for difference in means

$$\overline{d}-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{d}}< \mu_d < \overline{d}+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{d}}$$

## There are two ways to compare two means

* \alert{Paired $t$-test} provides a control for extraneous
variation and therefore have more power and precision.

* \alert{Two-sample $t$-tests} are often easier because you do not have to resample the same unit as in a paired comparison.

> In the *paired* design, both treatments are applied to every sampled unit. In the *two-sample* design, each treatment group is composed of an independent, random sample of units

## \alert{Two-sample $t$-test}

"Compare the means of two  of a numerical variable between two independent groups" when there is no natural pairing of samples

The sample sizes do not have to be the same in each group.

## Assumptions of \alert{Two-sample $t$-test}

* "Each of the two samples is a random sample from its population"
* "The numerical variable is normally distributed in each population"
* "The standard deviation (and variance) of the numerical variable is the same in both populations" (we will eventually relax this assumption)

## Cost of resistance to Aphids in lettuce

* Some lettuce genotypes are *Susceptible* and others are
*Resistant* to aphids.
* Why isn’t all lettuce resistant to aphids?
* Let us test the hypothesis that resistant lettuce has
lower fitness in the absence of aphids.
* Fitness = number of seeds per plant

| Genotype | $\overline{Y}_i$ | $s_i$ | $n_i$ |
|:--------:|:----------------:|:------|:-----:|
| Susceptible | 720 | 223.6 | 15 |
| Resistant | 582 | 277.3 | 16 |

# Parameter estimation and confidence intervals

## Standard error of the difference in means

| Genotype | $\overline{Y}_i$ | $s_i$ | $n_i$ |
|:--------:|:----------------:|:------|:-----:|
| Susceptible | 720 | 223.6 | 15 |
| Resistant | 582 | 277.3 | 16 |

The pooled sample variance is $s_p^2 = \frac{\mathit{df}_1 s_1^2 + \mathit{df}_2 s_2^2}{\mathit{df}_1 +\mathit{df}_2}$

$s^2_1$ is the sample variance of sample 1

$s^2_2$ is the sample variance of sample 2

$\mathit{df}_1 = n_1 - 1$; $\mathit{df}_2 = n_2 - 1$; 

total degrees of freedom for $t$ distribution: $\mathit{df} = \mathit{df}_1 +\mathit{df}_2$

$$s_p^2 = \frac{14 \times 223.6 ^2 + 15 \times 277.3^2}{14 + 15} = `r sprintf("%5f", (14 * 223.6 ^ 2 + 15 * 277.3 ^ 2)/29)`$$

## Standard error of the difference in means

| Genotype | $\overline{Y}_i$ | $s_i$ | $n_i$ |
|:--------:|:----------------:|:------|:-----:|
| Susceptible | 720 | 223.6 | 15 |
| Resistant | 582 | 277.3 | 16 |

The standard error of the difference in means is $\mathrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2} = \sqrt{s_p^2 (\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2})}$

$$\mathrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2} = \sqrt{63909.889310 (\frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{16})} = `r sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))`$$

## 95% confidence intervals for difference in means

$$(\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2)-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2} < (\mu_1 - \mu_2) < (\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2)+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2}$$

$\mathit{df} = 29$

$t_{0.05(2),\mathit{29}} = `r qt(0.975, 29)`$

Lower CI:

$$(720 - 582) - `r qt(0.975, 29)` \times `r sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))` = `r (720 - 582) - qt(0.975, 29) * sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))`$$

Upper CI:

$$(720 - 582) + `r qt(0.975, 29)` \times `r sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))` = `r (720 - 582) + qt(0.975, 29) * sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))`$$

## 95% confidence intervals for difference in means

We estimated the susceptible genotypes produce an average of 720 - 582 = 138 more seeds, but our 95% CI is -48 to 324. 

0 difference in fitness between genotypes is within the plausible range of values given our data.

# Hypothesis testing


## 1. Null and alternative hypotheses

$H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2$

$H_A$: $\mu_1 \ne \mu_2$

In our case, the mean fitness of resistant and susceptible lettuce genotypes is the same.

## 2. The $t$ test statistic

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}_1 - \overline{Y}_2}}$$

| Genotype | $\overline{Y}_i$ | $s_i$ | $n_i$ |
|:--------:|:----------------:|:------|:-----:|
| Susceptible | 720 | 223.6 | 15 |
| Resistant | 582 | 277.3 | 16 |

$$t = \frac{720 - 582}{`r sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16))`} = `r (720 - 582) / (sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16)))`$$

## 3. The $t$ distribution is the sampling distribution for $t$

Degrees of freedom: $\mathit{df}_1 = n_1 - 1$; $\mathit{df}_2 = n_2 - 1$; 

total degrees of freedom for $t$ distribution: $\mathit{df} = \mathit{df}_1 +\mathit{df}_2$


For our study, $(15 - 1) + (16 - 1) = 29$ degrees of freedom

The $t_{29}$ distribution looks like this:

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

test_stat <- (720 - 582) / (sqrt(63909.889310 * (1/15 + 1/16)))

df <- tibble(t = seq(-4, 4, 0.01), y = dt(t, 29))

alpha <- 0.05
critical_value <- qt(
  p = alpha / 2,
  df = 29, 
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = test_stat, size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[29])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```



## 4. $P$-values

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t > test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t < -test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(test_stat, -test_stat), color = "grey", size = 2) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[29])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```

## 4. $P$-values

For a two-tailed test (most common)

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}

P_value <- 2 * pt(
  q = 1.518867,
  df = 29,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

P_value
```

## 5. Decide

Since $P = `r round(P_value, 3)`$ is greater than $\alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

We don't have enough evidence to conclude that susceptible genotypes of lettuc have greater fitness than resistant genotypes in the absence of aphids.

## Difference between \alert{Two-sample $t$-test} and \alert{Welch's $t$-test}

\alert{Welch's $t$-test} does NOT assume "the standard deviation (and variance) of the numerical variable is the same in both populations"


## Difference between \alert{Two-sample $t$-test} and \alert{Welch's $t$-test}

\alert{Welch's $t$-test} is the default in *R*
